source.title_on_document: The Impact of Generative AI Dependence on University Students' Creativity: The Mediating Role of Critical Thinking and the Moderating Role of Thinking Orientation

supplement.holds: Materials only: Tables S1-S8 (Generative AI Dependence Scale, Self-Report Creativity Scale, Chinese Critical Thinking Structure Scale, AI Creativity Self-Efficacy Scale, outcome- and process-oriented priming statements, thinking-orientation manipulation-check items, CAT scoring rubrics) and the experimental task instructions for Studies 2 and 3. The listing names no statistical tables or standard errors, so all reported statistics are in the main text. The Study 3 task instructions may say whether ChatGPT was used in the Study 3 AUT.

paper_design_summary: Three studies of students at one Chinese university. Study 1 is a cross-sectional survey (142 students analyzed) that relates self-reported generative-AI dependence to self-reported creativity. In Study 2, 132 students were randomly assigned to a high-dependence arm (priming tasks done with mandatory ChatGPT answers, then told to adopt ChatGPT's solutions directly on an Alternative Uses Task) or a low-dependence arm (priming tasks done without tools, then told to use ChatGPT only as a supplementary reference on the same task), and three trained raters, blind to condition, scored the AUT responses with the Consensual Assessment Technique. In Study 3, 160 students were randomly assigned to a 2 x 2 of AI dependence (a trust-game instruction: fully trust the AI's investment advice vs exercise autonomous judgment) by thinking orientation (outcome vs process prime) before the same task, scored with the same measure; the Study 3 text does not say whether participants used ChatGPT or any AI on that task.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing assigned; one survey measured self-reported generative AI dependence, critical thinking, and creativity
assignment.quote: Study 1 aimed to preliminarily examine the relationship between generative AI dependence and university students’ creativity, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking, through a cross-sectional survey design.

ai_tool.how_used: No AI use in the study. Participants rated their own dependence on generative AI for academic research and study tasks (3-item scale of Tang et al. 2023).

outcomes.question: none

studies.label: Study 2 (AI dependence manipulation, AUT with ChatGPT)

assignment.what_was_assigned: High vs low AI dependence. Phase 1 priming: the high group had to use ChatGPT answers for three tasks and was told AI answers are optimal; the low group did the same tasks with no tools. Phase 2 AUT: both groups used ChatGPT; the high group was told to adopt ChatGPT's solutions directly, and the low group to use AI only as a supplementary reference and to complete its final solutions independently.
assignment.quote: A total of 132 university students (including graduate students; 51 males, 81 females) were recruited and randomly assigned to either the high-dependence group (n = 66) or the low-dependence group (n = 66).

arms.name: High AI dependence
arms.description: Phase 1 priming: strictly use ChatGPT-generated answers for three tasks (mathematical calculation, text summarisation, English translation), with instructions that 'the answers provided by the AI are optimal'. Phase 2 AUT: use ChatGPT and directly adopt the creative solutions it generates.

arms.name: Low AI dependence
arms.description: Phase 1 priming: the same three tasks done independently without any external tools (calculators, translation applications, search engines, or AI). Phase 2 AUT: use ChatGPT only as a supplementary reference and complete the final solutions independently.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper gives the actual sample as 132 participants (66 per group), and every Table 2 test uses t(130), consistent with all 132 analyzed.
participants.who: University students including graduate students; 51 males, 81 females; the groups did not differ in age, gender, or disciplinary background
participants.country: China (single institution per p. 12; Qufu Normal University is named for Study 1, p. 3, and as the ethics committee, p. 14)
participants.quote: The actual sample of 132 participants (66 per group) exceeded this minimum, ensuring adequate power for detecting the hypothesised group differences.
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 3.2 Sample size justification; p. 6, Table 2 (t(130))

ai_tool.how_used: Both arms used ChatGPT during the scored AUT, framed as a 'creative competition'. The high-dependence arm was told to directly adopt the creative solutions ChatGPT generated; the low-dependence arm was told to use AI only as a supplementary reference and to complete its final solutions independently (pp. 5-6). The paper does not describe the prompts. Tasks ran in a restricted computer environment (full-screen browser lockdown) with an experimenter present. The arms also differ in the Phase 1 priming task (mandatory ChatGPT answers vs no tools).

task.description: Alternative Uses Task framed as a 'creative competition': generate as many innovative uses as possible for a tennis racket and a water pipe.
task.duration: not_stated (single laboratory session; p. 13 calls the procedures single-session)

outcomes.name: Creativity index on the AUT (CAT, mean of three raters)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique (Amabile 1982): three psychology graduate students, after a 2 h calibration session on 20 pilot responses and blind to condition, independently scored each response on novelty, appropriateness, and fluency on 7-point scales; ICC = 0.86. The mean of the three raters' scores is the creativity index (p. 6). Dimension-level results are not reported. Rater type is borderline between expert and lay; the paper calls the Study 3 ratings 'expert-rated creativity' (p. 9).

contrasts.reported: Creativity: High AI Dependence 4.78 (0.66) vs Low AI Dependence 5.20 (0.53), SDs in parentheses; t(130) = 4.03, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.70 (Table 2 prints t and d as low minus high); 66 randomized and 66 analyzed per group (p. 5; no exclusions reported). Mediation via critical thinking: total effect c = -0.42, direct effect c' = -0.02, indirect effect ab = -0.40, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.70, -0.14].
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.3 Creativity performance, Table 2, and Mediation analysis; group ns p. 5

studies.label: Study 3 (2 x 2: AI dependence x thinking orientation, AUT)

Phase 3 is the AUT, 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2'; the Study 3 text does not restate AI use or AI instructions for that phase.

The only AI that the Study 3 text describes gives investment advice in the Phase 1 modified trust game on decision-making problems, which is not a creative task (role other); the paper does not say what kind of AI it is. The text does not say whether participants used ChatGPT or any AI during the Phase 3 AUT, or under which instructions: it says only that the task was 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2' (p. 8), where both arms used ChatGPT under different instructions. If Study 3 participants used ChatGPT on the AUT, the role is open_chat. Section 4 (pp. 7-10) never names ChatGPT. The supplement's Study 3 task instructions (not in this PDF) may settle it.

outcomes.name: Creativity index on the AUT (CAT, expert-rated, as in Study 2)
outcomes.question: not_stated
outcomes.measure_detail: Measured as in Study 2 ('Manipulation checks and dependent variable measures were the same as in the previous studies', p. 8): CAT by three trained raters on novelty, appropriateness, and fluency, 7-point scales, averaged. The paper calls it 'expert-rated creativity' (p. 9). The Table 4 regressions control for gender and year. AI availability during the Phase 3 AUT is not stated, so ai_available_when_produced, question, and the comparison type of all three contrasts are coded not_stated (codes the form-spec lists lack, used as other forms use them for unstated values). The text says only that the AUT was 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2' (p. 8), where both arms used ChatGPT under different instructions (pp. 5-6). Section 4 never names ChatGPT, and the discussion's 'does not require complete AI abstinence' and 'usage style' (p. 12) hint at AI use without stating it. Three readings remain. (1) ChatGPT on the AUT, with instructions that differ by AI-dependence condition: question with_ai, comparison ai_design, criterion 1 met for Study 3. (2) The AUT without AI: question after_ai, and the arms differ only in the Phase 1 trust-game instruction on decision-making problems, so criterion 1 fails for Study 3. (3) ChatGPT on the AUT under the same instructions in every cell: question with_ai, but criterion 1 again fails for Study 3. Reading of Table 4 (the paper prints the orientation coding only for Table 5, where W = 0 is outcome orientation): Model 2 has no interaction term, so its AI dependence term (B = -1.35) is pooled over orientation. Model 3 adds the interaction, so its AI dependence term (B = -1.54**, SE = 0.13) is the effect under outcome orientation and is filed with that contrast. Model 3 also prints Outcome/Process Orientation B = 1.00***, SE = 0.13; AI dependence x thinking orientation B = 0.39*, SE = 0.18 (under that coding, the process-oriented effect minus the outcome-oriented effect); R2 = 0.72, delta R2 = 0.01*. Arithmetic check, not printed in the paper: -1.54 matches the outcome-oriented cell gap 2.99 - 4.52 = -1.53, and -1.54 + 0.39 = -1.15 matches the process-oriented gap 4.40 - 5.55.

eligibility.reason: Study 2 meets all three criteria. It randomly assigns 132 students (66 per arm; all 132 analyzed, t(130)) to two configurations of ChatGPT use on the AUT: adopt ChatGPT's solutions directly vs use AI only as a supplementary reference (pp. 5-6). Both arms use ChatGPT while producing the scored output, so the contrast is ai_design. Three trained raters, blind to condition, score each AUT response with CAT (p. 6). Caveat: the arms also differ in a Phase 1 priming task (mandatory ChatGPT answers vs no tools), so the contrast bundles the priming with the usage instruction. Study 3 randomizes 160 students, analyzes 160 (Table 3 and 4 notes), and uses the same CAT outcome, but its AI-dependence factor is an instruction in a trust game on decision-making problems (fully trust the AI's investment advice vs exercise autonomous judgment), and its text does not say whether any arm used ChatGPT or other AI on the AUT (p. 8). Criterion 1 is therefore unclear for Study 3, and its arms' AI condition, its AI role, its outcome's AI availability and question, and its contrasts' comparison type are coded not_stated. Study 1 is a cross-sectional self-report survey and fails criteria 1 and 3. The paper is core through Study 2 whatever Study 3's coding turns out to be.

one_line_finding: In Study 2, students randomly told to adopt ChatGPT's AUT solutions directly scored lower on rater-scored creativity than students told to use ChatGPT only as a supplementary reference (4.78 vs 5.20, t(130) = 4.03, p < 0.001, d = 0.70; p. 6, Table 2), and in Study 3 students assigned to high AI dependence through a trust-game instruction scored lower under both thinking-orientation primes (Table 4, Model 2: B = -1.35, SE = 0.09; cell means 2.99 vs 4.52 outcome-oriented and 4.40 vs 5.55 process-oriented; p. 9).
open_questions: Study 3: the paper does not state whether participants used ChatGPT or any AI during the Phase 3 AUT, or under which instructions; it says only that the task was 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2' (p. 8). The discussion speaks of Study 3 'usage style' under high AI dependence (p. 12, Section 5.2) and says high-dependence participants were 'explicitly told to adopt AI outputs' after naming the manipulations in Studies 2 and 3 (p. 12, Section 5.3), which fits the trust-game instruction as well as an AUT instruction. The form therefore codes the S3 arms' ai, the S3 ai_tool.role, S3-O1's ai_available_when_produced and question, and the comparison type of the three S3 contrasts as not_stated. If participants used ChatGPT on the AUT under instructions that differ by AI-dependence condition, these become generative_ai, open_chat, yes, with_ai, and ai_design, and Study 3 meets criterion 1. If the AUT ran without AI, S3-O1 is after_ai and the role is other; if every cell used ChatGPT under the same instructions, S3-O1 is with_ai; in both cases criterion 1 fails for Study 3. The supplement's task instructions for Studies 2 and 3 (not in this PDF) may settle it.
Study 3: the trust-game 'AI investment advice' (p. 7) is not described. Whether it comes from a generative AI, and whether the low-dependence group also saw the advice, are not stated.
Study 3 setting (laboratory vs online) is not stated; lab_rct is kept by analogy to Study 2's laboratory procedure (p. 5).

Study 2's contrast bundles a Phase 1 priming difference (mandatory ChatGPT answers vs no tools) with the Phase 2 usage instruction. Coding it as ai_design is a judgment call; the authors say the manipulation combines reliance, trust, and reduced personal contribution (p. 5).

In Study 2's high-dependence arm participants were told to adopt ChatGPT's solutions directly, so the scored output is largely AI output, and the authors did not evaluate AI output quality (pp. 12-13). Reviewers may decide whether this contrast fits the pooled with_ai question.

Treatment and control: in the Study 2 ai_design contrast, and in the Study 3 contrasts (comparison type not_stated), high dependence (the manipulated configuration) is coded as treatment and low dependence (in Study 2, AI as a supplementary reference) as control. Reversing them makes the sign positive.
Rater type: three psychology graduate students after a 2 h calibration session; the paper calls the ratings 'expert-rated' (p. 9). expert_raters vs human_raters is a judgment call.

Study 3 process-oriented SDs (0.19 and 0.25) and d = 5.09 (p. 9) look implausible for CAT ratings, and the analyzed cell counts are not printed (the creativity simple-effects tests print t(77) for the 81 people randomized to the outcome-oriented cells). The audit can check both against the posted data (p. 14).
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the output: the AI-dependence and thinking-orientation manipulation checks, self-reported critical thinking (17-item Chinese Critical Thinking Structure Scale), and self-efficacy (3 items). Study 2, Table 2 (p. 6): critical thinking High 2.78 (0.29) vs Low 3.17 (0.28), t(130) = 7.94, d = 1.37; self-efficacy 3.45 (0.72) vs 3.52 (0.68), t(130) = 0.58, p = 0.566, d = 0.10; self-efficacy indirect effect -0.12, 95% CI [-0.40, 0.16] (p. 7). Study 3: critical-thinking regression in Table 3 (p. 8); conditional indirect effects in Table 5 (p. 10): outcome-oriented -0.18 (Boot SE 0.07) [-0.33, -0.05], process-oriented 0.05 (0.06) [-0.07, 0.17], index of moderated mediation 0.22 (0.10) [0.05, 0.43]. Reading of Table 4: Table 5 codes outcome orientation as W = 0, so the Model 3 AI dependence term (-1.54) is the effect under outcome orientation; it matches the outcome-oriented simple effect (2.99 vs 4.52). Model 2 has no interaction term, so its AI dependence term (-1.35) is pooled over orientation. The S3-O1 contrasts file the two terms that way. No diversity or homogenization outcome is reported. Studies 1 to 3 report separately recruited samples, and the paper does not say whether any student took part in more than one study. All participants come from a single institution (p. 12). IRB: Biomedical Ethics Committee of Qufu Normal University, protocol 2025093 (p. 14). The search record's note ('GenAI conditions without stated random assignment') does not hold for the full text, which states random assignment in Studies 2 and 3 (pp. 5, 7). Internal inconsistencies for the audit: (1) Study 2 Figure 3 (p. 7) prints paths 0.41***, -1.09**, and -0.38*** (0.06), which differ in sign and size from the text (a = -0.40, b = 1.01, c = -0.42, c' = -0.02; p. 6). (2) Study 1 Figure 2 (p. 4) prints -0.24***, 0.64***, (-0.13*), and 0.03, while the text gives total B = -0.22 and direct B = -0.07 (p. 4). (3) Study 3 simple-effects tests for creativity (p. 9) and critical thinking (pp. 8-9) are all printed as t(77), although 81 people (41 + 40) were randomized to the outcome-oriented cells (df 79 expected); the 79 people (39 + 40) randomized to the process-oriented cells match df 77. (4) Study 3 says the sample had '40 per cell' (p. 7), but the stated cells are 41, 39, 40, and 40. (5) Study 3 calls the process-orientation creativity gap 'substantially attenuated' but prints d = 5.09 against d = 1.95 under outcome orientation (p. 9); the raw mean gap is smaller under process orientation (1.15 vs 1.53), and d is larger there because the process-oriented SDs are small (0.19 and 0.25). (6) Study 3 AI-dependence manipulation-check means of 6.06 and 4.95 (p. 8) exceed the 5-point range given for the Tang et al. scale in Study 1 (p. 3), and Study 3 says the checks were the same as before (p. 8). (7) Table 4 Model 3 prints AI dependence B = -1.54 with SE 0.13 but only ** (p. 9); Table 3 Model 3 prints orientation B = 0.11 with SE 0.09 and * (p. 8). (8) Table 2 prints t and d as low minus high in every row, so the negative manipulation-check statistics (t = -3.45, d = -0.60, with high > low) follow that sign convention and are not an error (p. 6); screener B had listed them as an inconsistency. (9) Study 1 demographics appear twice on p. 3. (10) Study 2 says participants were told of the no-tools prohibition 'again before the creativity task in Phase 2', next to the statement that both groups used ChatGPT in Phase 2 (p. 5); the explicit Phase 2 description is taken as decisive.

open_items.item: Study 3: whether participants used ChatGPT or any AI on the Phase 3 AUT, and under which instructions (open question 1, and the one unresolved reconciliation difference, studies[2].ai_tool.role: A other, B open_chat). The text says only that the AUT was 'identical to the AUT used in Study 2' (p. 8). Until it is settled, the S3 arms' ai, its ai_tool.role, S3-O1's AI availability and question, and its contrasts' comparison type stay not_stated. It decides Study 3's criterion 1, and so whether Study 3 (160 analyzed) is a second core sample; the paper is core through Study 2 either way.

Study 3: the trust-game 'AI investment advice' (p. 7) is not described; whether it comes from a generative AI, and whether the low-dependence group saw the advice, are not stated (open question 2). It describes the Study 3 arms but decides no criterion, because the trust game is not a creative task. If the supplement's Study 3 instructions do not say, the authors.

Study 3 setting (laboratory vs online) is not stated; lab_rct is kept by analogy to Study 2's laboratory procedure (open question 3). Every randomized design class counts for criterion 1, so the setting changes only the design code. If the supplement's Study 3 instructions do not say, the authors.

Study 3 process-oriented SDs (0.19 and 0.25) and d = 5.09 (p. 9) look implausible for CAT ratings, and the analyzed cell counts are not printed (t(77) for the 81 people randomized to the outcome-oriented cells) (open question 8). They bear only on Study 3's effect sizes.

Study 2's contrast bundles the Phase 1 priming difference (mandatory ChatGPT answers vs no tools) with the Phase 2 usage instruction, so ai_design is a judgment call (open question 4). Both arms use ChatGPT on the AUT under different instructions, so criterion 1 holds either way; Review 1 decides the comparison type.

In Study 2's high-dependence arm the scored output is largely ChatGPT's, adopted as instructed, and the authors did not evaluate AI output quality (open question 5). Each participant still submits the response that the raters score, so criterion 3 holds; Review 1 decides whether the contrast fits the pooled with_ai question.

Treatment and control: high dependence is coded as treatment and low dependence as control, so the Study 2 effect is negative; reversing them flips the sign (open question 6). A coding convention for Review 1.

Rater type: three psychology graduate students after a 2 h calibration session, whose ratings the paper calls 'expert-rated' (p. 9); expert_raters vs human_raters is a judgment call (open question 7). People rate the output either way, so criterion 3 holds.
